about: MECH40009 Mechanics is a 5 ECTS core module in Year 1 of Imperial's MEng Mechanical Engineering, running from the autumn to the summer term (2026-27 programme specification). No public module descriptor (syllabus or assessment breakdown) was available, so the topics in this pack are a standard first-year statics and dynamics course built from the module's short description: free body diagrams and equilibrium, equivalent force systems, friction including threads, belts and clutches, particle kinematics and kinetics, rigid-body kinematics and relative motion in mechanisms. The department's 2026-27 module list also shows a separate core module, MECH40010 Foundational Mechanics, which does not appear in the programme specification; the two may overlap, so confirm with your department which module and content apply to you, and check the order and coverage against your lecture materials. Assessment details are not given here because they could not be confirmed.
topics: Particle kinetics: force, energy and momentum

notes.body:
Statics is the study of bodies that are not accelerating. It rests on Newton's laws: if the acceleration is zero, the resultant force and the resultant moment on the body must both be zero. The skill that matters most in this module is drawing a correct free body diagram (FBD).

Forces as vectors
- A force has magnitude, direction and a line of action. Resolve it into components: F_x = F cos θ, F_y = F sin θ, with θ measured from the x axis.
- Add forces by adding components, never by adding magnitudes (unless the forces are parallel).
- Newton's third law: the force A exerts on B is equal and opposite to the force B exerts on A. On FBDs of two connected parts, the contact forces appear with opposite arrows.

Equilibrium conditions
- Particle (all forces through one point): ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 (and ΣF_z = 0 in 3D).
- Rigid body in a plane: ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any point. That gives three independent equations.
- In 3D: six equations (three force, three moment).
- Choosing the moment point cleverly (where unknown forces act) removes unknowns from the equation.

Drawing a free body diagram
- Isolate the body completely: draw it alone, detached from supports and neighbours.
- Show every external force: weight at the centre of mass, applied loads, and the reaction at each support or contact.
- Reactions depend on the support: a smooth surface or roller gives one force normal to the surface; a pin gives two components (or a force of unknown direction); a fixed (built-in) support gives two force components and a couple; a cable gives a tension along the cable, pulling away from the body.
- Show dimensions and angles. If you guess a direction wrongly, the answer simply comes out negative.

Special cases
- Two-force member: a body with forces at only two points and no moments. The forces must be equal, opposite and along the line joining the points.
- Three-force member: three non-parallel forces in equilibrium must meet at a single point.
- Statically determinate: the number of unknown reactions equals the number of independent equilibrium equations. More unknowns means statically indeterminate (you need deformation, beyond this topic).

Worked example
A light beam AB, 4 m long, is simply supported at A and B and carries 10 kN at 1 m from A.
- Moments about A: R_B × 4 = 10 × 1, so R_B = 2.5 kN.
- Vertical forces: R_A = 10 − 2.5 = 7.5 kN. The nearer support carries more load.

Exam tips: always draw the FBD even if not asked (it usually earns marks), state your sign convention, and check your answer with an extra equilibrium equation, such as moments about a different point.

Two force systems are equivalent if they have the same resultant force and the same resultant moment about any point. Replacing a complicated set of loads with a simpler equivalent system is the basis of support calculations and of later work in stress analysis.

Moment of a force
- In 2D, the moment about point O is M_O = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action. Give a sense (clockwise or anticlockwise).
- In vector form M_O = r × F, where r runs from O to any point on the line of action. In 2D: M_z = x F_y − y F_x.
- Varignon's theorem: the moment of a force equals the sum of the moments of its components. This is often the easiest way to calculate moments.
- Principle of transmissibility: a force on a rigid body can slide along its line of action without changing its external effect.

Couples
- Two equal, opposite, parallel forces F a distance d apart form a couple of moment M = Fd.
- Its resultant force is zero, and its moment is the same about every point: a couple is a "free vector".
- Example: two 50 N forces 0.4 m apart give a 20 N m couple, whatever point you take moments about.

Moving a force
- A force F at point A is equivalent to the same force F at point B plus a couple equal to the moment of F (at A) about B. This is a force–couple system.

Reducing a system to a resultant
- Resultant force R = ΣF (vector sum).
- Resultant moment about O: M_O = Σ(r × F) + Σ(couples).
- In 2D, if R ≠ 0, the system reduces to a single force R along a line placed so that its moment about O equals M_O: perpendicular distance d = M_O/R.
- If R = 0 but M_O ≠ 0, the system reduces to a pure couple.
- In 3D the most general reduction is a wrench (a force plus a couple parallel to it).

Distributed loads
- A load w(x) (N/m) has resultant equal to the area under the load diagram, acting through the centroid of that area.
- Uniform load w over length L: resultant wL at L/2.
- Triangular load rising from zero to w₀ over L: resultant w₀L/2 acting L/3 from the high end (2L/3 from the zero end).
- Trapezoidal loads: split into a rectangle and a triangle.

Worked example
Forces on a beam along x: 200 N down at x = 0, 300 N down at x = 2 m, 100 N up at x = 5 m.
- R = 200 + 300 − 100 = 400 N down.
- M_O (anticlockwise positive) = 2(−300) + 5(100) = −100 N m, i.e. 100 N m clockwise.
- Single resultant position: −400 x̄ = −100, so x̄ = 0.25 m.

Exam tips: keep a consistent sign convention, find R first and then position it by matching moments, and check the answer by taking moments about a second point.

Friction resists sliding between surfaces in contact. In machines it is sometimes a loss (bearings, screws) and sometimes the whole point (belts, clutches, brakes).

Coulomb (dry) friction
- The friction force F acts along the contact surface, opposing the relative sliding (or the impending sliding).
- No slip: F is whatever equilibrium requires, up to a limit F ≤ μ_s N.
- Impending slip: F = μ_s N. Sliding: F = μ_k N, with μ_k usually a little below μ_s.
- Friction is roughly independent of the apparent contact area and of sliding speed.
- Angle of friction φ: tan φ = μ. The total reaction (normal plus friction) is inclined at up to φ from the normal.
- A block on an incline is on the point of slipping under its own weight when tan θ = μ_s, so θ = φ. With μ_s = 0.3 this is about 16.7°.
- Problems: decide whether slip is impending, and in which direction, before writing F = μN. If unsure, assume no slip, solve for F and check F ≤ μ_s N.

Wedges
- Draw FBDs of each part, with friction on every sliding face opposing the motion that would occur.

Square-threaded screws (screw jack)
- A thread is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder. The lead L is the axial advance per turn; mean radius r.
- Lead angle α: tan α = L/(2πr).
- Torque to raise load W: M = W r tan(φ + α).
- Torque to lower: M = W r tan(φ − α) if φ > α.
- Self-locking (the load does not unwind on its own) if φ > α.
- Efficiency in raising = tan α/tan(α + φ). A self-locking screw always has efficiency below 50 %.
- V-threads behave as if μ were increased to μ/cos β, where β is the thread half-angle.

Flat belts and ropes over pulleys
- For a belt on the point of slipping round angle of wrap β (radians): T₁/T₂ = e^(μβ), with T₁ the tight side.
- Example: μ = 0.3, β = π, T₂ = 100 N gives T₁ ≈ 257 N.
- Power transmitted P = (T₁ − T₂)v, where v is the belt speed.
- V-belts wedge into the groove, which raises the effective coefficient to μ/sin(half-angle of the groove).

Disc (plate) clutches
- Friction torque depends on how pressure is distributed over the annulus (inner radius r_i, outer r_o).
- Uniform pressure (new clutch): T = (2/3)μF(r_o³ − r_i³)/(r_o² − r_i²) per friction surface.
- Uniform wear (worn-in clutch): T = μF(r_o + r_i)/2 per friction surface. This gives slightly lower torque, so it is the conservative design assumption.
- Multiply by the number of friction surfaces (a single plate gripped on both faces has two).
- Example: μ = 0.3, F = 4 kN, r_o = 150 mm, r_i = 100 mm gives 150 N m per surface (uniform wear) or 152 N m (uniform pressure).

Exam tips: always state whether slip is impending, mark which belt side is tight, and use radians in e^(μβ).

Kinematics describes motion (position, velocity and acceleration) without asking what causes it. A particle is a body whose size and rotation do not matter for the problem.

Rectilinear (straight-line) motion
- v = ds/dt and a = dv/dt = d²s/dt². Also a = v dv/ds, which is useful when a is given as a function of position.
- Constant acceleration only: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t.
- If a varies (with time, position or velocity), integrate: for a(t), v = u + ∫a dt and s = ∫v dt; for a(v), separate variables, dt = dv/a(v).
- Example: a = 2t m/s², v(0) = 3 m/s, s(0) = 0 gives v = 3 + t² and s = 3t + t³/3; at t = 3 s, v = 12 m/s and s = 18 m.
- Graphs: the slope of s–t is v, the slope of v–t is a, and the area under v–t is the displacement.

Curvilinear motion: choosing coordinates
- Cartesian (x, y): good when the accelerations along fixed axes are known, as in projectiles.
- Normal and tangential (n–t): good for motion along a known path.
- Polar (r–θ): good when motion is described from a fixed pivot, such as a slider on a rotating arm.

Projectiles (no air resistance)
- a_x = 0, a_y = −g. Treat horizontal and vertical motions separately; they share the same time.
- Launched at speed v at angle θ on level ground: time of flight 2v sin θ/g; maximum height (v sin θ)²/(2g); range v² sin 2θ/g, greatest (v²/g) at 45°.
- Example: 20 m/s at 30° gives a range of 35.3 m and a maximum height of 5.10 m.

Normal–tangential components
- Velocity is always tangential: v = v e_t.
- a_t = dv/dt (change of speed); a_n = v²/ρ (change of direction), directed towards the centre of curvature; ρ is the radius of curvature.
- Total acceleration magnitude √(a_t² + a_n²). A particle moving at constant speed round a curve still accelerates.

Polar components
- v_r = ṙ, v_θ = rθ̇.
- a_r = r̈ − rθ̇² and a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇.
- The 2ṙθ̇ term is the Coriolis term. It appears whenever the distance from the pivot changes while the line rotates. You will meet it again in mechanisms.

Relative motion of particles
- r_B = r_A + r_B/A, so v_B = v_A + v_B/A and a_B = a_A + a_B/A (for translating reference frames).

Exam tips: choose the coordinate system that matches how the problem is described, and only use the constant-acceleration equations after checking that the acceleration really is constant.

notes.h: Particle kinetics: force, energy and momentum
notes.body:
Kinetics links motion to its causes. There are three routes, all from Newton's second law. Choosing the right one saves a lot of algebra.

Newton's second law (force and acceleration)
- ΣF = ma, applied in whatever coordinates suit the problem: Cartesian, n–t (ΣF_n = mv²/ρ, ΣF_t = m dv/dt) or polar.
- Draw a free body diagram and a kinetic diagram (showing ma). Remember that ma is not a force: there is no "centrifugal force" on a correct FBD in an inertial frame.
- For connected bodies (pulleys, strings), write the law for each body and add the kinematic constraint linking their accelerations.
- Best when you need accelerations or forces at an instant.

Work and energy
- Work done by a force: U = ∫F·ds. Only the component along the motion does work. Normal reactions on fixed smooth surfaces do no work.
- Kinetic energy T = ½mv². Work–energy principle: T₁ + U₁→₂ = T₂.
- Conservative forces (gravity, springs) have potential energy: V_g = mgh, V_e = ½kx². If only conservative forces do work, T + V is constant.
- Friction does negative work μ_k N × distance, and the energy is lost as heat.
- Power P = F·v = dU/dt; efficiency = power out/power in.
- Best when forces depend on position and you want speeds, not times.

Worked example
A block slides from rest 5 m down a 30° slope with μ_k = 0.2.
- Work by gravity: mg × 5 sin 30°. Work against friction: 0.2 mg cos 30° × 5.
- ½mv² = mg × 5(sin 30° − 0.2 cos 30°), giving v² = 32.1 and v ≈ 5.66 m/s (the mass cancels).

Impulse and momentum
- Linear impulse ∫F dt equals the change in linear momentum mv. It is a vector equation.
- Best when forces act for known times or when you need speeds after impacts.
- If no external impulse acts on a system, its total momentum is conserved (collisions, explosions, recoil).

Direct central impact
- Momentum is conserved along the line of impact: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
- Coefficient of restitution e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂): the speed of separation divided by the speed of approach. e = 1 is perfectly elastic (no kinetic energy lost); e = 0 is perfectly plastic (bodies move together).
- Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest with e = 0.5. Then v₁ = 1.5 m/s, v₂ = 3 m/s, and 2.25 J of kinetic energy is lost.

Angular momentum of a particle
- H_O = r × mv. A central force (always through O) gives zero moment, so H_O is conserved: this explains why orbiting bodies speed up nearer the centre.

Exam tips: state which principle you are using and why, include every force that does work (or exerts an impulse), and treat momentum as a vector, minding the signs when a body rebounds.

A rigid body has size and can rotate, so we need angular as well as linear quantities. This topic covers plane motion, where every point moves parallel to a fixed plane.

Types of plane motion
- Translation: every line in the body keeps its direction; all points have the same velocity and acceleration.
- Rotation about a fixed axis: points move in circles about the axis.
- General plane motion: a combination of translation and rotation (rolling wheels, connecting rods).

Rotation about a fixed axis
- Angular position θ, angular velocity ω = dθ/dt, angular acceleration α = dω/dt. For a rigid body these are the same for every line in the body.
- Constant α: ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ (the same forms as linear motion).
- A point at radius r: speed v = ωr; tangential acceleration a_t = αr; normal (centripetal) acceleration a_n = ω²r = v²/r, towards the axis.
- Vector form: v = ω × r and a = α × r − ω²r (for plane motion).
- Convert rpm to rad/s by multiplying by 2π/60. Example: a flywheel reaching 1200 rpm (125.7 rad/s) from rest in 10 s has α = 12.6 rad/s² and turns 100 revolutions.

General plane motion: relative velocity
- For any two points A and B on the body: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A.
- The relative velocity of B with respect to A is perpendicular to AB with magnitude ω × AB: from A's viewpoint, B can only rotate.
- This is the basis of velocity diagrams for mechanisms (next topic).

Instantaneous centre of rotation (ICR)
- At any instant there is a point (possibly off the body) with zero velocity; the body is momentarily rotating about it.
- To find it, draw lines perpendicular to the known velocity directions of two points: the ICR is where they cross.
- Then every point's speed is ω × (its distance from the ICR), directed perpendicular to the line joining it to the ICR.
- The ICR generally has a non-zero acceleration, so do not use it for accelerations.

Rolling without slipping
- A wheel of radius r rolling on a fixed surface: the contact point is the ICR, so the centre moves at v = ωr.
- The top of the wheel moves at 2v; points level with the centre move at √2 v.
- The centre's acceleration is αr along the surface; the contact point accelerates towards the centre at ω²r.

Relative acceleration
- a_B = a_A + α × r_B/A − ω²r_B/A: a tangential part (αr, perpendicular to AB) and a normal part (ω²r, from B towards A).

Exam tips: use the ICR for quick velocity answers, but use the relative-acceleration equation for accelerations. Always draw the geometry at the instant in question.

Mechanisms (slider-cranks, four-bar linkages, quick-return mechanisms) are assemblies of rigid links. Their velocities and accelerations are found by applying the relative-motion equations link by link, either as vector algebra or as velocity and acceleration diagrams.

Velocity analysis
- Start from a link whose motion is known, usually a crank OA rotating at ω about a fixed pivot: v_A = ω × OA, perpendicular to OA.
- For the next link AB: v_B = v_A + v_B/A, where v_B/A is perpendicular to AB with magnitude ω_AB × AB.
- A constraint fixes the direction of v_B (a slider moves along its guide; a rocker end moves perpendicular to its link).
- Graphically: draw v_A to scale, then a line perpendicular to AB through its tip, and a line in the known direction of v_B from the origin. The intersection gives v_B and v_B/A.
- Then ω_AB = |v_B/A|/AB, with its sense found from the direction of v_B/A.

Acceleration analysis
- Each relative acceleration of points on the same link has two parts:
- Centripetal: ω_AB² × AB, directed from B towards A. This is known once the velocities are known.
- Tangential: α_AB × AB, perpendicular to AB, magnitude unknown.
- a_B = a_A + (a_B/A)_n + (a_B/A)_t. With the direction of a_B known (for a slider), the unknowns are a_B and α_AB, so the vector equation can be solved.
- A crank at constant speed still has a_A = ω²r towards O.

Sliding contact on a rotating link: the Coriolis term
- When a point P slides along a link that is itself rotating at ω, the acceleration of P relative to a fixed frame is
- a_P = a_coincident point on link + a_rel + 2ω × v_rel.
- The Coriolis acceleration 2ω × v_rel has magnitude 2ωv_rel and is perpendicular to the link (v_rel rotated 90° in the sense of ω).
- In polar form this is the 2ṙθ̇ term. Example: a collar moving outward at 2 m/s along an arm rotating at 5 rad/s has a Coriolis component of 20 m/s².
- Forgetting it is the most common error in quick-return and slotted-link problems.

The slider-crank
- Crank radius r, connecting rod length l, crank angle θ from the line of stroke.
- Rod angle φ: sin φ = (r/l) sin θ.
- Piston position x = r cos θ + √(l² − r² sin² θ).
- Piston velocity and acceleration follow from differentiating, or from the vector method, which is usually clearer in exams.
- At θ = 0° and 180° the piston is at rest (dead centres) and the rod's angular velocity is greatest.

Four-bar linkages
- Grashof's condition (s + l ≤ p + q, for shortest s, longest l and other links p and q) tells you whether a link can fully rotate.

Exam tips: set up position vectors carefully at the instant given, solve velocities completely before attempting accelerations, and list every acceleration component (centripetal, tangential, Coriolis) before solving.

cards.f: Conditions for equilibrium of a rigid body in a plane
cards.b: ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any point: three independent equations.
A sketch of the body isolated from its surroundings showing all external forces and moments acting on it, with dimensions.
Two force components (or one force of unknown direction), no moment.
Two force components plus a couple (moment).
A body loaded at only two points with no moments: the forces are equal, opposite and collinear along the line joining the points.
Three non-parallel forces in equilibrium must be concurrent (meet at one point).
More unknown reactions than independent equilibrium equations; equilibrium alone cannot find them.
M_O = F × perpendicular distance from O to the line of action; vector form M = r × F, M_z = xF_y − yF_x.
The moment of a force about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components about that point.
Two equal, opposite, parallel forces; zero resultant force and the same moment Fd about every point.
A force moved to a new point must be accompanied by a couple equal to its moment about the new point.
A force on a rigid body can be moved along its line of action without changing its external effect.

cards.b: wL acting at the mid-point of the loaded length.
w₀L/2 acting at the centroid: L/3 from the high end, 2L/3 from the zero end.
The simplest general 3D force system: a resultant force with a couple parallel to it.
F ≤ μ_s N with no slip; F = μ_s N at impending slip; F = μ_k N while sliding.
φ with tan φ = μ; a block slips down an incline under its own weight when the slope exceeds φ.
tan α = L/(2πr), where L is the lead (advance per turn) and r the mean radius.
Raise: M = Wr tan(φ + α). Lower: M = Wr tan(φ − α). Self-locking if φ > α.
T₁/T₂ = e^(μβ) at impending slip, with β the wrap angle in radians and T₁ the tight side.
P = (T₁ − T₂)v, where v is the belt speed.
T = μF(r_o + r_i)/2 per friction surface; the usual conservative design assumption.
T = (2/3)μF(r_o³ − r_i³)/(r_o² − r_i²) per friction surface.
v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, s = ½(u + v)t; valid only for constant a.

cards.f: Acceleration as a function of position
cards.b: Use a = v dv/ds and integrate: ∫v dv = ∫a(s) ds.
R = v² sin 2θ/g; maximum v²/g at θ = 45° (no air resistance).
a_t = dv/dt (speed change); a_n = v²/ρ towards the centre of curvature (direction change).
v_r = ṙ, v_θ = rθ̇.
a_r = r̈ − rθ̇²; a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇ (the 2ṙθ̇ term is the Coriolis term).
The area under the velocity–time graph.
T₁ + U₁→₂ = T₂: initial kinetic energy plus work done by all forces equals final kinetic energy.

e = (speed of separation)/(speed of approach) along the line of impact; e = 1 elastic, e = 0 plastic.
P = F·v, the rate of doing work; for torque, P = Mω.

cards.f: Why normal reactions on fixed smooth surfaces do no work
cards.b: They are perpendicular to the displacement, so F·ds = 0.

cards.f: Conservation of angular momentum of a particle
cards.b: If the resultant force always passes through O (central force), H_O = r × mv is constant.
A sketch of the ma (or Iα) terms, drawn beside the FBD to set ΣF equal to ma.

cards.f: Speed and accelerations of a point on a rotating body
cards.b: v = ωr; a_t = αr (tangential); a_n = ω²r towards the axis.

cards.f: Relative velocity on a rigid body
cards.b: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A; the relative part is perpendicular to AB with magnitude ω·AB.
The point of zero velocity at an instant; found where perpendiculars to two known velocity directions intersect.
Contact point is the ICR; v_centre = ωr; top point moves at 2v_centre.
Multiply by 2π/60; e.g. 1200 rpm ≈ 125.7 rad/s.

cards.f: Why not use the ICR for accelerations
cards.b: The ICR's position changes and it generally has non-zero acceleration, so a = ω²r about it is wrong.

cards.f: Relative acceleration on a rigid body
cards.b: a_B = a_A + α × r_B/A − ω²r_B/A: tangential αr plus centripetal ω²r towards A.

cards.f: Relative velocity of two points on one link
cards.b: Perpendicular to the line joining them, magnitude ω_link × length.
ω_AB² × AB, directed from B towards A along the link.
α_AB × AB, perpendicular to the link; usually the unknown in an acceleration diagram.
2ω × v_rel for a point sliding along a rotating link; magnitude 2ωv_rel, perpendicular to the link.
sin φ = (r/l) sin θ, for crank radius r, rod length l and crank angle θ.
Crank in line with the rod (θ = 0° or 180°): piston velocity zero.
s + l ≤ p + q (shortest plus longest ≤ sum of the other two) for at least one link of a four-bar to rotate fully.

questions.q: A light beam AB of span 4 m is simply supported at both ends and carries a 10 kN load 1 m from A. What is the reaction at A?
questions.why: Moments about B: R_A × 4 = 10 × 3, so R_A = 7.5 kN. 2.5 kN is R_B; it comes from taking moments about B but using the 1 m distance measured from A. 5 kN splits the load equally, which is only true for a central load. 10 kN gives the whole load to one support, ignoring the other.

questions.q: A 100 N weight hangs from a ring held by two cables, each at 30° above the horizontal on opposite sides. What is the tension in each cable?
questions.why: Vertical equilibrium: 2T sin 30° = 100, so T = 100 N. 50 N shares the weight equally but ignores the fact that the cables are inclined, so only their vertical components hold the weight. 57.7 N uses cos 30°, which treats the 30° as measured from the vertical. 200 N is 100/sin 30°, as if a single cable carried the whole weight.

questions.q: A light horizontal beam AB, 2 m long, is pinned to a wall at A. End B is held by a cable to point C on the wall 1.5 m directly above A. A 600 N load hangs from B. Draw the free body diagram and find the cable tension and the pin reaction at A.
markScheme: FBD: pin components A_x, A_y at A; tension T along BC; 600 N at B
Cable angle to beam: tan θ = 1.5/2, θ = 36.9° (sin 0.6, cos 0.8)
A_x = T cos θ = 800 N (pushing the beam away from the wall)
questions.modelAnswer: The FBD of the beam shows A_x and A_y at the pin, the cable tension T acting along BC (up and towards the wall), and 600 N down at B. The cable makes angle θ with the beam where tan θ = 1.5/2, so sin θ = 0.6 and cos θ = 0.8 (θ ≈ 36.9°). Moments about A: the vertical component of T, 0.6T, acts at 2 m; the horizontal component passes through A. So 0.6T × 2 = 600 × 2, giving T = 1000 N. Horizontal: A_x = 0.8 × 1000 = 800 N, acting away from the wall to balance the cable's pull towards it. Vertical: A_y + 0.6 × 1000 − 600 = 0, so A_y = 0. This makes sense: the beam is then a two-force member, with the pin force along the beam.

questions.q: Two equal and opposite parallel forces of 50 N act 0.4 m apart on a rigid body. What is their combined moment about a point 1 m from the nearer line of action (and so 1.4 m from the other)?
questions.why: This is a couple, so its moment is Fd = 50 × 0.4 = 20 N m about any point; directly, 50 × 1.4 − 50 × 1 = 20 N m. 120 N m adds the two moments (70 + 50) as if they turned the same way, but the opposite forces turn in opposite senses. 10 N m uses half the separation (0.2 m) as the arm. 0 N m confuses zero resultant force with zero moment; the forces cancel as forces but not as moments.

questions.q: A distributed load rises linearly from zero at one end to 6 kN/m at the other over a 3 m length. What is its resultant?
options: 9 kN acting 2 m from the zero end
18 kN acting 1.5 m from the zero end
9 kN acting 1.5 m from the zero end
9 kN acting 1 m from the zero end
questions.why: The resultant is the triangle's area, ½ × 6 × 3 = 9 kN, acting through its centroid, two thirds of the length from the zero end (2 m). 18 kN at 1.5 m treats the load as uniform at its peak value. 9 kN at 1.5 m has the right size but puts it at the midpoint, which is only right for a uniform load. 1 m from the zero end is the one-third point measured from the wrong end.

questions.q: A horizontal beam lies along the x axis from O. It carries 200 N downwards at x = 0, 300 N downwards at x = 2 m and 100 N upwards at x = 5 m. (a) Replace the system by a force–couple system at O. (b) Replace it by a single resultant force and give its position.
markScheme: So 100 N m clockwise at O (with 400 N down)
Single force 400 N down at x̄ with 400x̄ = 100
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Resultant force: −200 − 300 + 100 = −400 N, i.e. 400 N downwards. Moments about O (anticlockwise positive, M = xF_y): 0 × (−200) + 2 × (−300) + 5 × 100 = −100 N m. So at O the system is equivalent to 400 N downwards plus a 100 N m clockwise couple. (b) A single 400 N downward force at x̄ has moment −400x̄ about O. Setting −400x̄ = −100 gives x̄ = 0.25 m. Check about the point x = 2 m, using M = (x − 2)F_y: the original forces give (−2)(−200) + 0 + 3(100) = 700 N m, and the single force gives (0.25 − 2)(−400) = 700 N m. They agree.

questions.q: A block rests on a plane whose slope is slowly increased. The coefficient of static friction is 0.3. At what slope angle does the block start to slide?
questions.why: At impending slip mg sin θ = μmg cos θ, so tan θ = 0.3 and θ = 16.7°. 17.5° is arcsin 0.3, which sets sin θ = μ by dropping the cos θ in the normal force. 72.5° is arccos 0.3, another wrong inverse function. 73.3° is 90° − 16.7°, the correct angle but measured from the vertical instead of the horizontal.

questions.q: A flat belt wraps half way (180°) round a pulley with μ = 0.3. The slack-side tension is 100 N. What is the largest tight-side tension before the belt slips?
questions.why: T₁ = T₂e^(μβ) = 100e^(0.3π) ≈ 257 N, with β = π radians. 194 N uses the linear approximation 1 + μβ instead of the exponential. 135 N is 100e^(0.3), which leaves out the wrap angle. 39 N divides by e^(μβ), treating the given 100 N as the tight side.

questions.q: A screw jack has a single-start square thread with mean radius 10 mm and lead 5 mm. The coefficient of friction is 0.15 and the load is 10 kN. Ignoring collar friction, find (a) the torque to raise the load, (b) whether the jack is self-locking, (c) the torque to lower it, and (d) the efficiency when raising.
markScheme: Lower: M = Wr tan(φ − α) ≈ 6.96 N m
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Lead angle: tan α = 5/(2π × 10) = 0.0796, so α ≈ 4.55°. Friction angle φ = arctan 0.15 ≈ 8.53°. Raising torque M = Wr tan(φ + α) = 10 000 × 0.010 × tan 13.08° ≈ 23.2 N m. (b) φ = 8.53° > α = 4.55°, so the jack is self-locking: the load will not unwind it. (c) Lowering torque M = Wr tan(φ − α) = 100 × tan 3.98° ≈ 6.96 N m (positive, confirming that effort is needed to lower). (d) Efficiency = tan α/tan(α + φ) = 0.0796/0.2324 ≈ 0.34, i.e. about 34 %, below 50 % as expected for a self-locking screw.

questions.q: A ball is projected at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal over level ground (g = 9.81 m/s², no air resistance). How far away does it land?
questions.why: R = v² sin 2θ/g = 400 × sin 60°/9.81 = 35.3 m. 40.8 m is v²/g, the maximum range at 45°, so the launch angle has been ignored. 20.4 m uses sin θ instead of sin 2θ. 17.7 m is half the range, the horizontal distance to the highest point, as if the flight ended at the apex.

questions.q: A car travels round a bend of radius 50 m at 20 m/s while speeding up at 6 m/s². What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
questions.why: a_n = v²/ρ = 400/50 = 8 m/s² and a_t = 6 m/s². They are perpendicular, so |a| = √(8² + 6²) = 10 m/s². 14 m/s² adds the components as scalars, ignoring that they are at right angles. 8 m/s² is the normal component alone. 2 m/s² subtracts the tangential component from the normal one, as if they acted along the same line in opposite directions.

questions.q: A particle moves along a straight line with acceleration a = 2t m/s². At t = 0 it is at s = 0 with velocity 3 m/s. Find its velocity and position at t = 3 s, and explain why the constant-acceleration equations cannot be used.
markScheme: a varies with time, so suvat equations do not apply
questions.modelAnswer: Acceleration depends on time, so the constant-acceleration (suvat) equations are invalid and we must integrate. v = 3 + ∫₀ᵗ 2t dt = 3 + t². s = ∫₀ᵗ (3 + t²) dt = 3t + t³/3. At t = 3 s, v = 3 + 9 = 12 m/s and s = 9 + 9 = 18 m. (Using suvat with the final acceleration of 6 m/s² would give s = 9 + 27 = 36 m, which is wrong.)

questions.q: A block slides from rest 5 m down a 30° slope with μ_k = 0.2 (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is its speed at the bottom?
questions.why: v² = 2gL(sin 30° − μ cos 30°) = 2 × 9.81 × 5 × 0.327 ≈ 32.1, so v ≈ 5.66 m/s. 7.00 m/s ignores friction altogether. 5.42 m/s takes the friction force as μmg, forgetting that the normal force on a slope is mg cos θ. 8.67 m/s swaps sin and cos, which treats the slope as if it were at 60°.

questions.q: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 6 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse from the wall?
questions.why: Impulse = change in momentum = 0.2 × (6 − (−10)) = 3.2 N s, because the velocity reverses direction. 0.8 N s subtracts the speeds (10 − 6) without accounting for the reversal. 2.0 N s is only the incoming momentum, as if the ball stopped dead. 1.2 N s is only the rebound momentum.

questions.q: A 2 kg sphere moving at 3 m/s collides directly with a 1 kg sphere at rest. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. Find the velocities after impact and the kinetic energy lost.
markScheme: Solve: v₁ = 1.5 m/s, v₂ = 3.0 m/s (both in original direction)
questions.modelAnswer: Momentum: 6 = 2v₁ + v₂. Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = e(u₁ − u₂) = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5. Substituting v₂ = v₁ + 1.5 gives 6 = 3v₁ + 1.5, so v₁ = 1.5 m/s and v₂ = 3.0 m/s, both in the original direction. Kinetic energy before: ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J. After: ½ × 2 × 1.5² + ½ × 1 × 3² = 2.25 + 4.5 = 6.75 J. Energy lost = 2.25 J (25 %), dissipated as heat, sound and permanent deformation.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 0.3 m rolls without slipping with its centre moving at 6 m/s. How fast is the topmost point of the rim moving?
questions.why: The contact point is the ICR and the top is 2r from it, so v = ω × 2r = 20 × 0.6 = 12 m/s. 6 m/s treats the wheel as purely translating, ignoring its rotation. 0 m/s is the speed of the contact point, not the top. 8.49 m/s (√2 × 6) is the speed of a point on the rim level with the centre, √2 r from the contact point.

questions.q: A flywheel accelerates uniformly from rest to 1200 rpm in 10 s. How many revolutions does it make in that time?
questions.why: Average speed 600 rpm = 10 rev/s, for 10 s, gives 100 revolutions. 200 uses the final speed for the whole 10 s, ignoring that it started from rest. 6000 multiplies the average speed in rpm by the time in seconds, without converting minutes to seconds. 628 is the angle in radians (½αt² = ½ × 12.57 × 100), reported as revolutions without dividing by 2π.

questions.q: A rod AB of length 1 m slides with end A on a horizontal floor and end B against a vertical wall. At the instant when the rod makes 60° with the floor, A moves away from the wall at 2 m/s. Use the instantaneous centre to find the angular velocity of the rod and the velocity of B.
markScheme: ICR at intersection of the vertical through A and the horizontal through B
Distance ICR to A = height of B = sin 60° = 0.866 m
Distance ICR to B = horizontal distance of A from wall = cos 60° = 0.5 m
questions.modelAnswer: A moves horizontally, so the ICR lies on the vertical line through A; B moves vertically, so the ICR lies on the horizontal line through B. With the wall–floor corner at O, A is 1 × cos 60° = 0.5 m from the wall and B is 1 × sin 60° = 0.866 m up the wall. The ICR is therefore at the corner of the rectangle opposite O, 0.866 m above A and 0.5 m from B. ω = v_A/0.866 = 2/0.866 ≈ 2.31 rad/s. v_B = ω × 0.5 ≈ 1.15 m/s, directed down the wall. Check by differentiating x² + y² = 1: xẋ + yẏ = 0, so ẏ = −0.5 × 2/0.866 = −1.15 m/s.

questions.q: A crank of length 0.1 m rotates at a constant 30 rad/s. What is the acceleration of the crank pin?
questions.why: At constant ω there is no tangential component, and the centripetal part is ω²r = 900 × 0.1 = 90 m/s² towards the pivot. 9000 m/s² is ω²/r, dividing by the radius instead of multiplying. 3 m/s² is ωr, which is the pin's speed in m/s, not an acceleration. 'Away from the pivot' gives the direction of the fictitious centrifugal force rather than the real acceleration.

questions.q: A collar slides outward at 2 m/s relative to a straight arm rotating at a constant 5 rad/s. What is the magnitude of the Coriolis component of the collar's acceleration?
options: 0, because the sliding is purely radial
questions.why: Coriolis acceleration = 2ωv_rel = 2 × 5 × 2 = 20 m/s², perpendicular to the arm. 10 m/s² misses the factor of 2. Purely radial sliding is exactly the case that produces a Coriolis term, so zero is wrong. 50 m/s² is ω²v_rel, which is dimensionally inconsistent (its units are m/s³).

questions.q: A slotted arm rotates about a fixed pivot at a constant 4 rad/s. A collar moves outward along it at a constant 1.5 m/s relative to the arm. At the instant the collar is 0.5 m from the pivot, find its velocity and acceleration (magnitude and components).
markScheme: Coriolis term identified as the whole of a_θ here
questions.modelAnswer: Use polar components with r = 0.5 m, ṙ = 1.5 m/s, r̈ = 0, θ̇ = 4 rad/s, θ̈ = 0. Velocity: v_r = 1.5 m/s outward and v_θ = 0.5 × 4 = 2 m/s, so |v| = 2.5 m/s. Acceleration: a_r = r̈ − rθ̇² = 0 − 0.5 × 16 = −8 m/s², i.e. 8 m/s² towards the pivot (centripetal). a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇ = 0 + 2 × 1.5 × 4 = 12 m/s² in the direction of rotation; this is entirely the Coriolis component. |a| = √(64 + 144) ≈ 14.4 m/s². Note the collar has a large acceleration even though both rates are constant.

questions.q:
A uniform ladder 5 m long and weighing 300 N rests against a smooth vertical wall with its foot on rough horizontal ground (μ_s = 0.4). It makes 60° with the ground.
(a) Draw the free body diagram of the ladder with a person of weight 800 N standing a distance s up the ladder. [4]
(b) Find how far up the ladder the person can climb before it slips. [7]
(c) Find the smallest angle with the ground at which the unloaded ladder can stand without slipping. [4]
(d) Find the smallest angle at which the person could reach the top of the ladder safely. Comment on your answer. [5]
markScheme: (a) FBD: wall reaction N_W horizontal (smooth); ground N_G up and friction F towards wall; 300 N at mid-length; 800 N at s
(b) Vertical: N_G = 1100 N; horizontal: F = N_W; slip when F = 0.4 × 1100 = 440 N
(b) Moments about foot: N_W × 5 sin 60° = 300 × 2.5 cos 60° + 800 s cos 60°
(c) Unloaded: N_W × L sin θ = W(L/2) cos θ, F = N_W ≤ μW ⇒ tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ) = 1.25 ⇒ θ ≥ 51.3°
(d) Person at top: 440 × 5 sin θ = (750 + 4000) cos θ ⇒ tan θ = 2.16 ⇒ θ ≈ 65.1°
(d) Comment: steeper ladder needs less friction; at 60° the person can only reach 3.83 m; practical guidance and safety margin
Clear sign convention and check of equilibrium
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Forces on the ladder: at the top, a horizontal normal reaction N_W from the smooth wall (no friction there); at the foot, a vertical normal reaction N_G and a friction force F acting towards the wall (the foot tends to slide outwards); the ladder's weight 300 N at its mid-point; and the person's 800 N at distance s along the ladder from the foot.

(b) Vertical equilibrium: N_G = 300 + 800 = 1100 N. Horizontal: F = N_W. At impending slip F = μN_G = 0.4 × 1100 = 440 N, so N_W = 440 N. Moments about the foot (the wall reaction acts at height 5 sin 60° = 4.330 m; the weights act at horizontal distances measured along the ground): N_W × 4.330 = 300 × 2.5 cos 60° + 800 × s cos 60°. So 440 × 4.330 = 1905 = 375 + 400s, giving s ≈ 3.83 m. The person can climb about 3.8 m of the 5 m ladder before it slips.

(c) Unloaded: N_G = 300 N, so F ≤ 120 N. Moments about the foot: N_W × 5 sin θ = 300 × 2.5 cos θ, so N_W = 150/tan θ. Requiring N_W = F ≤ 120 gives tan θ ≥ 1.25, so θ ≥ 51.3° (the general result tan θ = 1/(2μ)).

(d) With the person at the top (s = 5 m) and slip impending, N_W = 440 N: 440 × 5 sin θ = (300 × 2.5 + 800 × 5) cos θ = 4750 cos θ. So tan θ = 4750/2200 ≈ 2.16 and θ ≈ 65.1°. A steeper ladder reduces the moment of the weights about the foot and so reduces the wall reaction and the friction needed. At 60° the ladder would need μ ≈ 0.50 for the person to reach the top. In practice ladders are set at about 75° and footed or tied, which gives a safety margin over this idealised calculation (the real wall is not perfectly smooth, and μ is uncertain).

questions.q:
In a slider-crank mechanism the crank OA is 100 mm long and rotates anticlockwise at a constant 100 rad/s. The connecting rod AB is 400 mm long and the slider B moves along a horizontal line through O. Consider the instant when the crank is at 60° above the line of stroke (measured from OB).
(a) Find the angle of the connecting rod and the position vectors of A and B relative to O, and of B relative to A. [4]
(b) Find the velocity of A, the angular velocity of AB and the velocity of the slider. [8]
(c) Find the acceleration of A, the angular acceleration of AB and the acceleration of the slider. [10]
(d) Explain how your answers to (b) would change at the inner dead centre, θ = 180°. [3]
markScheme: (b) v_B = v_A + ω_AB k × r_B/A; y: 0 = 5.00 + 0.3905ω_AB ⇒ ω_AB ≈ −12.8 rad/s (clockwise)
(c) a_B = a_A + α_AB k × r_B/A − ω_AB² r_B/A with ω_AB² ≈ 163.9 s⁻²
(d) At θ = 180° the slider is momentarily at rest (v_B = 0) and |ω_AB| = rω/l = 25 rad/s, its maximum
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) sin φ = (r/l) sin θ = (0.1/0.4) × 0.866 = 0.2165, so φ ≈ 12.5° (the rod slopes down from A to B). With O at the origin: r_A = 0.1(cos 60°, sin 60°) = (0.050, 0.0866) m. x_B = r cos θ + √(l² − r² sin² θ) = 0.05 + √(0.16 − 0.0075) = 0.05 + 0.3905 = 0.4405 m, so r_B = (0.4405, 0) and r_B/A = (0.3905, −0.0866) m.

(b) For a rotation ω about z, ω k × (x, y) = ω(−y, x). v_A = 100(−0.0866, 0.050) = (−8.66, 5.00) m/s, magnitude 10 m/s, perpendicular to OA. v_B = v_A + ω_AB k × r_B/A = (−8.66, 5.00) + ω_AB(0.0866, 0.3905). The slider moves horizontally, so the y component is zero: 5.00 + 0.3905ω_AB = 0, giving ω_AB ≈ −12.8 rad/s (12.8 rad/s clockwise). x component: v_B = −8.66 + 0.0866 × (−12.8) = −8.66 − 1.11 ≈ −9.77 m/s, i.e. 9.77 m/s towards O.

(c) The crank speed is constant, so a_A = −ω²r_A = −10 000(0.050, 0.0866) = (−500, −866) m/s², magnitude 1000 m/s² towards O. For the rod: a_B = a_A + α_AB k × r_B/A − ω_AB² r_B/A. ω_AB² = 163.9 s⁻², so −ω_AB² r_B/A = (−64.0, +14.2) m/s², and α_AB k × r_B/A = α_AB(0.0866, 0.3905). y component (slider has no vertical acceleration): −866.0 + 0.3905α_AB + 14.2 = 0, so α_AB ≈ 851.8/0.3905 ≈ 2180 rad/s², anticlockwise. x component: a_B = −500 + 0.0866 × 2180 − 64.0 ≈ −500 + 188.9 − 64.0 ≈ −375 m/s², i.e. about 375 m/s² towards O. (Differentiating x(θ) twice gives the same result, which is a useful check.)

(d) At θ = 180° the crank and rod are in line, so v_A is vertical and perpendicular to the line of stroke. The slider is momentarily at rest (v_B = 0), and v_B/A must cancel v_A, so the rod has its largest angular velocity in magnitude: |ω_AB| = rω/l = 0.1 × 100/0.4 = 25 rad/s. The slider is at the end of its stroke and about to reverse.
